headline: Against the odds, endangered dolphins survive in Bangladesh's polluted river
meta_description: Around 20 Ganges river dolphins persist in the Buriganga, one of the world's five most polluted rivers, offering hope for conservation.
summary_short: Despite toxic heavy metals and industrial waste, about 20 endangered Ganges river dolphins continue to thrive in Bangladesh's heavily polluted Buriganga River.
body:
In one of the world's most contaminated urban rivers, an unexpected discovery offers a glimmer of hope for conservation. A 12-month study of the Buriganga River—a 29-kilometre waterway that flows past Dhaka city—found approximately 20 Ganges river dolphins living in waters so toxic that native fish species have virtually vanished. The river, ranked among the five most polluted globally, absorbs daily discharges of toxic industrial effluent from hundreds of factories, tanneries, and pharmaceutical plants, along with untreated sewage. Heavy metals including chromium, lead, and cadmium regularly exceed safety limits set by the World Health Organization. Yet dolphins not only survived there; researchers documented calves accounting for nearly 16 percent of sightings, indicating that reproduction continues despite the extreme pollution.

The dolphins appear to be hunting invasive suckermouth catfish—among the few species tolerant enough to inhabit these waters. Researchers tracked the dolphins across a 27-kilometre stretch throughout most months, with sightings peaking in December and the winter season. "When we found them, we were amazed at how it was possible," researcher Md. Aminur Rahman told Mongabay. "Because the river is not livable for fish."

The Buriganga's dolphins are part of a larger recovery effort across Bangladesh. A recent survey conducted by the country's Forest Department and WCS Bangladesh recorded 2,307 Ganges river dolphins across 45 rivers between 2024 and 2025. However, conservation remains precarious. Experts emphasize that protecting these dolphins requires urgent action: controlling pollution and curbing harmful fishing practices like illegal gill nets, which trap and kill dolphins. Without intervention, even these resilient survivors may not endure.
quick_facts: Around 20 Ganges river dolphins live in Bangladesh's Buriganga River
Buriganga ranks among the five most polluted rivers in the world
Heavy metals including chromium, lead, and cadmium exceed WHO safety limits
Nearly 16% of dolphin sightings were calves, showing ongoing reproduction
2,307 Ganges river dolphins recorded across 45 Bangladesh rivers in 2024–2025
